questions.q: A novel follows a penniless teenage narrator who survives by working for a series of employers, each a target of satire, and he ends much the same as he began. What kind of story is it?
choices: A quest
A bildungsroman
A picaresque
A well-made play
questions.explain: A low-born rogue, a string of masters, satire, and little inner change: the pattern of Lazarillo de Tormes.

questions.q: How does Don Quixote relate to the quest and the picaresque?
choices: It's a straight Grail romance with no comedy
It parodies the knightly quest, sending its hero through the low, episodic world of the picaresque
It invented the picaresque, which Lazarillo de Tormes later copied
It's a bildungsroman ending in accommodation
questions.explain: Quixote imagines a chivalric quest, but rides through inns, roads and con men; Cervantes even has a galley slave mention Lazarillo.

questions.q: A script reader says your road movie's episodes could be shuffled without anything breaking. Which old criticism is this?
choices: Aristotle's: the plot is episodic, without probability or necessity
Bergson's: the characters are mechanical
Freytag's: there's no exciting force
Vonnegut's: the line is flat
questions.explain: Aristotle called plots where events merely follow one another episodic, and the worst kind.

questions.q: Which fix would most help an episodic road story gain momentum?
choices: Adding more locations
Giving each episode a different tone
Adding a destination with a deadline, or a relationship that changes along the way
Removing the companion so the hero is alone
questions.explain: An engine running under every episode (a clock, a hidden question, a developing bond) makes the sequence matter.

questions.q: What holds Tom Jones together, despite its road-novel inns and adventures?
choices: A single location, like a farce
The hidden question of Tom's parentage, which pays off at the end
A narrator who never leaves home
A Grail that must be found
questions.explain: Fielding's tight plotting around the secret of Tom's birth is why Coleridge ranked it among the most perfect plots.

questions.q: In Huckleberry Finn, what gives the raft journey a true climax?
choices: Huck's moral decision not to betray Jim
Arriving at the mouth of the Mississippi
Tom Sawyer's elaborate rescue plan
The King and the Duke's last con
questions.explain: The inner journey, Huck deciding whether to turn Jim in, runs under the episodes and peaks when he tears up the letter.

questions.q: A reporter follows a teenager's real route north to reunite with his mother, retracing the journey herself. What gives this kind of journalism its momentum?
choices: The inverted pyramid's ranking of facts
The destination: every stop is a step toward or away from it
A nut graf in every section
The reporter's own coming of age
questions.explain: In a journey narrative like Enrique's Journey, the destination supplies the pull; the stops supply the reporting.

ideas: Which approach sends a low-born rogue down the road from master to master, satirizing each, without changing him much?
Which approach gets its pull from a destination or a sought-after object that turns out to matter less than the search?
Which approach risks episodic drift, and fixes it with a clock, a companion or a hidden question?
Which approach puts strangers in a car or bus, so the miles and the relationship change together?
